title: Post-intubation hypotension
trigger: New hypotension after RSI, tube placement, or positive-pressure ventilation.
immediateMoves: Confirm pulse, blood pressure, waveform, oxygenation, and tube depth.
Auto-PEEP/dynamic hyperinflation plausible: disconnect briefly.
Reduce excessive PEEP or tidal volume while maintaining oxygenation.
Suspected preload dependence: crystalloid bolus 500-1000 mL IV.
Push-dose epinephrine 5-20 mcg IV every 2-5 minutes. Mix 1 mL of 0.1 mg/mL (cardiac) epinephrine into 9 mL saline for 10 mcg/mL. Give 0.5-2 mL per dose.
Start norepinephrine early, 0.05-0.1 mcg/kg/min, titrated to MAP.
Consider tension pneumothorax, mainstem intubation, hemorrhage, sepsis, or peri-intubation arrest physiology.
reassess: Repeat BP every 1-2 minutes until stable
avoid: Do not assume the tube is the only problem.
Keep analgesia and sedation going while the patient is paralyzed. Lower the dose if the pressure is low.
references: Heffner AC, et al. Incidence and factors associated with cardiac arrest complicating emergency airway management. Resuscitation. 2013;84(11):1500-1504. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.resuscitation.2013.07.022
Russotto V, et al. Intubation Practices and Adverse Peri-intubation Events in Critically Ill Patients (INTUBE). JAMA. 2021;325(12):1164-1172. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2021.1727

Acquisto NM, et al. Society of Critical Care Medicine Clinical Practice Guidelines for Rapid Sequence Intubation in the Critically Ill Adult Patient. Crit Care Med. 2023;51(10):1411-1430. https://doi.org/10.1097/CCM.0000000000006000
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Failed airway / cannot intubate
trigger: Failed attempts, falling oxygen saturation, poor view, inability to ventilate, or airway contamination.
immediateMoves: Call the failed-airway plan out loud and assign roles.
Reoxygenate: two-hand BVM, oral/nasal airway, PEEP valve, suction.
Change something before the next attempt: operator, blade, position, device, bougie, or approach. Maximum three attempts plus one by a more experienced operator, then declare failed intubation.
Failed intubation or failing BVM: second-generation supraglottic airway now, up to three attempts.
Cannot oxygenate by facemask or SGA: ensure full neuromuscular block, then front-of-neck access.
avoid: Do not repeat the same failed attempt.
Do not spend the last 30 seconds of failing oxygenation debating.
references: Ahmad I, et al. Difficult Airway Society 2025 guidelines for management of unanticipated difficult tracheal intubation in adults. Br J Anaesth. 2026;136(1):283-307. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bja.2025.10.006
Difficult Airway Society. DAS airway algorithms. https://das.uk.com/guidelines/das_intubation_guidelines
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Arterial puncture during central line
trigger: Bright pulsatile blood, arterial waveform, high-pressure tubing, or ultrasound concern during access.
immediateMoves: Stop. Control the wire or catheter. Do not dilate while position is uncertain.
If stable enough, transduce it. Color, pulsatility and a blood gas do not settle it.

Needle, wire or 18 G catheter, not dilated, any site: remove it. Compress 5-10 min where compressible, longer if anticoagulated. Neck site: watch the airway. Subclavian or axillary: cannot be compressed, so watch for hemothorax.
Dilator or larger catheter in an artery, any site including subclavian or axillary: leave it in place, cap or transduce, call vascular/IR now.
Document the event, site, exam, and consultation.
reassess: Airway compression risk for neck sites
avoid: Do not pull a dilator or larger catheter out of an artery and hold pressure. It stays in until vascular or IR remove it.
references: Bowdle A. Vascular complications of central venous catheter placement: evidence-based methods for prevention and treatment. J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth. 2014;28(2):358-368. https://doi.org/10.1053/j.jvca.2013.02.027
Guilbert MC, et al. Arterial trauma during central venous catheter insertion: case series, review and proposed algorithm. J Vasc Surg. 2008;48(4):918-925. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jvs.2008.04.046
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Lost guidewire / wire control problem
trigger: Wire no longer visible or control of the proximal wire is lost.
immediateMoves: Stop the procedure.
Wire end still visible: clamp it with a hemostat, keep hold, and withdraw. Resists withdrawal: hold it and image. Do not force it.
Do not advance the catheter or dilator blindly.
Not immediately retrievable: image to localize the wire.
Call IR/vascular per local resources.
File a safety event and document it.
avoid: Do not conceal the event.
references: Vannucci A, et al. Retained guidewires after intraoperative placement of central venous catheters. Anesth Analg. 2013;117(1):102-108. https://doi.org/10.1213/ANE.0b013e3182599179

The Joint Commission. Sentinel Event Alert: preventing unintended retained foreign objects. https://www.jointcommission.org/resources/sentinel-event/sentinel-event-alert-newsletters/sentinel-event-alert-issue-51-preventing-unintended-retained-foreign-objects/
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Failed transvenous pacer capture
trigger: Pacer spikes without electrical/mechanical capture, persistent bradycardia, or unstable hypotension.
immediateMoves: Check the generator is on, rate appropriate, output high, connections secure.
Generator on and connected, but no spikes or pauses: oversensing. Reduce sensitivity (raise the mV setting). Still inhibited, or no time: asynchronous (VOO).
Increase mA until capture, then set a safety margin above threshold.
No capture at maximum output: reposition. Deflate, withdraw a few centimeters, reinflate, refloat.
Position confirmed, still no capture: hyperkalemia, acidosis, hypoxia or a class I drug is raising the threshold. Treat it (calcium for hyperkalemia).
Hiccups or diaphragmatic pacing, new chest pain, or hypotension after a good capture: suspect perforation. Do not advance. Echo for an effusion.
Advance or withdraw the catheter slowly while watching the ECG and pulse/BP. Deflate the balloon before any withdrawal.
Confirm the course with ultrasound, fluoro, or CXR if available.
Continue transcutaneous pacing while troubleshooting.

Hypotensive: epinephrine infusion 2-10 mcg/min or dopamine 5-20 mcg/kg/min. Bridge with push-dose epinephrine 5-20 mcg IV every 2-5 minutes. Mix 1 mL of 0.1 mg/mL (cardiac) epinephrine into 9 mL saline for 10 mcg/mL. Give 0.5-2 mL per dose.
avoid: Do not accept electrical spikes as success without a pulse/BP response.
references: Glikson M, et al. 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronization therapy. Eur Heart J. 2021;42(35):3427-3520. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehab364
American Heart Association. Part 9: Adult Advanced Life Support, 2025 CPR and ECC Guidelines. https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-advanced-life-support
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Procedural sedation apnea
trigger: Hypoventilation, apnea, desaturation, loss of airway tone, or rising ETCO2 during sedation.
immediateMoves: Stop sedative dosing and call for airway help.
Reposition the airway, jaw thrust, suction. Oral or nasal airway as needed.
BVM with PEEP if ventilation is inadequate.

Reverse only when appropriate to the agent and context, and never instead of ventilating. Opioid: naloxone 0.04-0.4 mg IV, titrated every 2-3 minutes. Benzodiazepine: flumazenil 0.2 mg IV over 15 seconds, repeated to 1 mg. No flumazenil with chronic benzodiazepine use, seizure disorder, or a proconvulsant co-ingestion such as a TCA (seizure risk).
Prepare for intubation if oxygenation or ventilation cannot be maintained.
avoid: Do not wait on the pulse oximeter while the patient is not ventilating.
references: American Society of Anesthesiologists. Practice Guidelines for Moderate Procedural Sedation and Analgesia. Anesthesiology. 2018;128(3):437-479. https://doi.org/10.1097/ALN.0000000000002043

American College of Emergency Physicians. Clinical Policy: Procedural Sedation and Analgesia in the Emergency Department. Ann Emerg Med. 2014;63(2):247-258. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.annemergmed.2013.10.015
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)
trigger: Early warning - stop injecting and reassess: perioral numbness or tingling (lips, mouth, tongue), ringing in the ears or tinnitus, metallic taste, light-headedness, blurred or double vision, drowsiness, agitation or confusion.
Established toxicity: seizure, altered mental status, dysrhythmia, or cardiac arrest. May occur immediately or up to 60 minutes after injection.
Under sedation or general anesthesia the prodrome may be absent or unobservable. A dysrhythmia or sudden hypotension can be the first sign. Absence of early symptoms does not exclude LAST.
immediateMoves: Stop injecting local anesthetic.
Call for 20% lipid emulsion (Intralipid) now.
Seizure or loss of consciousness: secure the airway early, high-flow O2, prepare to intubate.
Cardiac arrest: ACLS with lipid emulsion started at the same time. Epinephrine sparingly, in ≤1 mcg/kg doses. Alert ECMO or cardiopulmonary bypass early. Prolonged CPR is justified.

Lipid emulsion 20%. >70 kg: 100 mL over 2-3 min, then 200-250 mL over 15-20 min. <70 kg: 1.5 mL/kg over 2-3 min, then 0.25 mL/kg/min (ideal body weight). Still unstable: repeat the bolus once or twice and double the infusion. Continue at least 10 min after circulatory stability. Max ~12 mL/kg.
Seizure: benzodiazepine, midazolam 1-2 mg IV or 0.05 mg/kg, repeatable.
reassess: Rhythm and BP every 1-2 minutes until stable
Response to lipid emulsion. The endpoint is cardiac recovery
SpO2 and ETCO2 continuously if intubated
avoid: No vasopressin. No calcium-channel blockers, beta-blockers or local anesthetics (lidocaine, procainamide) for dysrhythmias (ASRA).
Do not use propofol for seizures or in place of lipid emulsion: it is a myocardial depressant and its lipid is too dilute.
Do not assume resolution is complete. Cardiovascular toxicity can recur. Observe ≥4-6 hours after a cardiovascular event, ≥2 hours after a CNS-only event.
No high-dose epinephrine: ≤1 mcg/kg doses.
references: Neal JM, et al. The Third American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine Practice Advisory on Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity. Reg Anesth Pain Med. 2018;43(2):113-123. https://doi.org/10.1097/AAP.0000000000000720

Di Gregorio G, et al. Clinical presentation of local anesthetic systemic toxicity: a review of published cases, 1979 to 2009. Reg Anesth Pain Med. 2010;35(2):181-187. https://doi.org/10.1097/AAP.0b013e3181d2310b

ASRA Pain Medicine. Checklist for Treatment of Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity. 2020. https://www.asra.com/guidelines-articles/original-articles/article-item/asra-news/2020/11/01/checklist-for-treatment-of-local-anesthetic-systemic-toxicity
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Pneumothorax after central venous catheter
trigger: Respiratory distress, hypoxia, or decreased breath sounds after IJ, subclavian, or axillary central venous catheter placement.
immediateMoves: Assess vital signs, SpO2, bilateral breath sounds, JVD, tracheal position.
Ultrasound: absent lung sliding on the line side suggests pneumothorax. A lung point confirms it.
Tension physiology (hypotension with absent breath sounds or lung sliding on the line side): needle decompression now, without waiting for imaging. JVD and tracheal deviation are often absent.
Large or symptomatic without tension: chest tube or pigtail catheter.
Small and asymptomatic, not on positive-pressure ventilation: supplemental O2, serial imaging, close monitoring in a monitored setting.
On positive-pressure ventilation: chest tube regardless of size.
reassess: Vital signs and SpO2 every 15 minutes
Repeat CXR at 4-6 hours for an observed small pneumothorax
Response to chest tube drainage: air leak on water seal, lung re-expansion
avoid: Do not dismiss absent lung sliding on the side of a subclavian or IJ line as artifact.
Do not attempt a contralateral central line before the ipsilateral pneumothorax is secured.
Do not clamp a chest tube with a suspected ongoing air leak without expert guidance.
references: Hind D, et al. Ultrasonic locating devices for central venous cannulation: meta-analysis. BMJ. 2003;327(7411):361. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.327.7411.361
Roberts ME, et al. British Thoracic Society Guideline for pleural disease. Thorax. 2023;78(Suppl 3):s1-s42. https://doi.org/10.1136/thorax-2022-219784
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Chest tube malposition
trigger: Poor drainage, persistent air leak, respiratory deterioration, pain out of proportion, or imaging showing the tube in a fissure, subcutaneous tissue, or abdomen after chest tube or pigtail catheter placement.
immediateMoves: CXR now: tube position, residual pneumothorax or effusion, relation to the diaphragm.
Exclude a kinked, clamped, or obstructed circuit before calling it malposition.
Subcutaneous tube (no drainage, crepitus along the tube): remove and replace.
Tube in the major or minor fissure: may drain slowly. Replace it or add a second tube if drainage is inadequate.

Tube through the diaphragm into the abdomen: stop drainage now. Do not pull it without surgical consultation. Remove it only with a surgeon present and a vascular injury plan (intra-abdominal hemorrhage risk).
Tube in the heart, a great vessel or the mediastinum: leave it in, clamp it, cardiothoracic surgery now.
Place a new tube in the safe triangle for the original indication.
reassess: Drainage output and character every 1-2 hours after repositioning
Air leak: bubbling in the water seal. Tidaling with respiration shows a patent tube in the pleural space
Repeat CXR after repositioning or replacement
avoid: Do not advance a chest tube after placement. It carries a non-sterile segment into the pleural space.
Do not clamp for a suspected large bronchopleural fistula without expert guidance (tension pneumothorax risk).
references: Kwiatt M, et al. Thoracostomy tubes: a comprehensive review of complications and related topics. Int J Crit Illn Inj Sci. 2014;4(2):143-155. https://doi.org/10.4103/2229-5151.134182
Roberts ME, et al. British Thoracic Society Guideline for pleural disease. Thorax. 2023;78(Suppl 3):s1-s42. https://doi.org/10.1136/thorax-2022-219784
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Laryngospasm
trigger: Sudden partial or complete glottic closure during or after sedation, airway manipulation, or extubation.
Partial: stridor. Complete: silent obstruction, paradoxical chest movement, desaturation.
immediateMoves: Stop all airway stimulation: suctioning, airway manipulation, and the precipitating procedure.
100% O2 by tight-fitting BVM mask, with jaw thrust and chin lift.
Larson's point: firm bilateral pressure in the laryngospasm notch (behind the ramus, in front of the mastoid) with jaw thrust.
CPAP with the BVM, 10-20 cmH2O.
Not breaking within 30-60 seconds: succinylcholine 0.1-0.2 mg/kg IV (subparalyzing dose). Prepare for possible intubation.
No IV: succinylcholine 4 mg/kg IM (max 150 mg). That is a full paralyzing dose with slow onset, so bag and prepare to intubate. IO: the IV dose.
Child with bradycardia: oxygenate and give atropine 0.02 mg/kg IV, IO or IM (max 0.5 mg).
Complete obstruction and impending arrest: succinylcholine 1-2 mg/kg IV and intubate. Surgical airway ready.
reassess: Chest rise with each positive-pressure breath. None means complete closure
Heart rate: bradycardia signals impending cardiac arrest
avoid: Do not force a laryngoscope or airway device through a closed glottis.
Do not delay succinylcholine if BVM ventilation is failing.
Do not sedate with ketamine without suction at hand. Secretions can precipitate laryngospasm.
references: Gavel G, Walker RWM. Laryngospasm in anaesthesia. Contin Educ Anaesth Crit Care Pain. 2014;14(2):47-51. https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkt031
Larson CP. Laryngospasm - the best treatment. Anesthesiology. 1998;89(5):1293-1294. https://doi.org/10.1097/00000542-199811000-00056
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Air embolism during central or large-bore access
trigger: Sudden hypoxia, hypotension, chest pain, altered consciousness, or cardiovascular collapse around an open hub - at insertion, while a line is disconnected, or at removal.
immediateMoves: Occlude the hub or open lumen now: clamp, cap, or cover the site.
Left lateral decubitus, head down. Focal deficit or seizure (arterial gas): flat supine instead.
100% oxygen.
Central lumen already in place with a central tip: aspirate from it.
Support the circulation: IV fluid bolus, and norepinephrine 0.05-0.1 mcg/kg/min titrated to MAP or push-dose epinephrine 5-20 mcg IV every 2-5 minutes.
Arrested: CPR supine. Compressions can also break up a large air lock.
Call for help. Consider hyperbaric referral for suspected cerebral arterial gas embolism.
reassess: SpO2 and end-tidal CO2 (a sudden ETCO2 fall fits a large embolism)
Neurological status, including a focal deficit suggesting arterial gas embolism
avoid: Do not leave a large-bore sheath or catheter hub open to air at any point, including removal.
Do not sit the patient up.
Do not delay occluding the hub for imaging.
references: Mirski MA, et al. Diagnosis and treatment of vascular air embolism. Anesthesiology. 2007;106(1):164-177. https://doi.org/10.1097/00000542-200701000-00026
McCarthy CJ, et al. Air embolism: practical tips for prevention and treatment. J Clin Med. 2016;5(11):93. https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm5110093
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Re-expansion pulmonary edema after pleural drainage
trigger: Repetitive cough, chest tightness or pain, or worsening breathlessness during or shortly after pleural drainage. Usually after a large or rapid volume, but it can follow a small one.
immediateMoves: Stop draining and clamp the drain. Slowing it is not enough. Bubbling drain (air leak) or hemothorax: do not clamp. Take it off suction, water seal only. Hemothorax output still counts toward the surgical triggers.
Sit the patient up. High-flow oxygen titrated to saturation.
Clamped drain: do not reopen it this session. If more fluid must come off later, drain slowly and stop at the first symptom.
Escalate early: CPAP or non-invasive ventilation for hypoxia that does not correct. Intubation with lung-protective settings if it progresses.
Support the circulation with fluids and, if needed, norepinephrine 0.05-0.1 mcg/kg/min titrated to MAP.
Chest x-ray: unilateral edema on the drained side. Exclude pneumothorax as the cause.
reassess: SpO2 and work of breathing every 5 minutes until stable
Drain clamped and staying clamped, or on water seal if bubbling or a hemothorax
avoid: Do not give diuretics reflexively. This is permeability edema rather than volume overload, and they may worsen hypovolemia.
Do not attribute new hypoxia after drainage to the effusion without excluding pneumothorax.
Do not use vacuum bottles or wall suction for therapeutic aspiration. Suction increases this risk.
references: Roberts ME, et al. British Thoracic Society Guideline for pleural disease. Thorax. 2023;78(Suppl 3):s1-s42. https://doi.org/10.1136/thorax-2022-219784
Sohara Y. Reexpansion pulmonary edema. Ann Thorac Cardiovasc Surg. 2008;14(4):205-209. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18818568/
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Orbit still tense after canthotomy
trigger: Canthotomy made but the orbit has not decompressed: globe still tense and proptotic, intraocular pressure still raised, vision or pupil not improved.
Lower lid does not swing freely away from the globe when pulled outward and downward: incomplete release.
immediateMoves: Treat as an incomplete inferior cantholysis until proven otherwise.
Clear the field with gentle pressure and gauze before cutting again.
Grasp the lower lid with toothed forceps, pull outward and downward to tension the inferior crus, and strum for the taut band running to the lateral orbital rim.
Cut the remaining inferior crus with blunt-tipped scissors aimed at the orbital rim, inferiorly and slightly posteriorly, away from the globe. The lid should then swing freely and the globe soften.
Reassess: orbital tension, intraocular pressure, proptosis, vision or at least light perception, and the pupil.
Release the superior crus only if, after a complete inferior release, all three persist: orbit tense, pressure raised, vision or pupil not improved. It adds lacrimal artery and gland risk.
Call ophthalmology emergently. Continue medical measures to lower intraocular pressure under their guidance. Do not wait for either to finish the release.
reassess: Whether the lower lid swings freely away from the globe
Globe tension and proptosis on gentle palpation
Intraocular pressure if a tonometer is available
Vision or light perception and the pupil, after each release
Time from symptom onset to decompression
avoid: Do not stop at the skin incision. Without the cantholysis the orbital pressure is unchanged.
Do not go to the superior crus to make up for an incomplete inferior release, which is far commoner than a genuine need to go superior.
Do not cut toward the globe, and do not substitute sharp or iris scissors for blunt-tipped ones in a swollen, bloody field.
Suspected globe rupture: stop manipulating the orbit and get emergent ophthalmology.
references: Rowh AD, et al. Lateral canthotomy and cantholysis: emergency management of orbital compartment syndrome. J Emerg Med. 2015;48(3):325-330. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jemermed.2014.11.002
U.S. Joint Trauma System. Eye Trauma: Initial Care Clinical Practice Guideline. 2021. https://jts.health.mil/assets/docs/cpgs/Eye_Trauma_Initial_Care_01_Jun_2021_ID03.pdf
American Academy of Ophthalmology EyeWiki. Orbital Compartment Syndrome. https://eyewiki.aao.org/Orbital_Compartment_Syndrome
Verify local institutional policy, the ophthalmology consultation pathway, and which blunt scissors are stocked on the eye tray.

title: Needle position uncertain during pericardiocentesis
trigger: Blood in the syringe, or blood that clots briskly, with no proof of tip position - before dilating, passing a wire, or railroading a catheter.
Bright pulsatile return, new ventricular ectopy as the needle advances, or a tip not seen in the fluid pocket on ultrasound.
immediateMoves: Stop. Do not dilate or railroad a catheter until position is proven.
Aspirate color does not confirm position. In hemopericardium everything is blood.
Agitated saline: inject a few milliliters. Bubbles in the pericardial space confirm position. Bubbles in a cardiac chamber mean the tip is in the heart.

Saline contrast unavailable or equivocal: see the needle, wire, or catheter in the pericardial space on real-time ultrasound, or transduce the hub. A ventricular pressure waveform means the tip is in the ventricle.
Brisk clotting in the syringe supports intracardiac blood but never confirms it. Pericardial blood is usually defibrinated.
Intracardiac: withdraw the needle, watch, and re-scan for a new or enlarging effusion. A needle hole usually seals.
Dilator or catheter already in a chamber: leave it in, cap it, activate cardiothoracic surgery and blood now.
Then re-plan rather than repeat: largest pocket, shortest safe path, depth read off the screen, advance under real-time visualization.
Activate cardiothoracic surgery and blood if the effusion enlarges or the patient deteriorates.
reassess: Where the bubbles went on agitated saline
Wire seen inside the pericardial space before dilating, and the catheter seen there after placement
Rhythm and blood pressure - new ectopy suggests the tip is against or in myocardium
Repeat ultrasound for a new or enlarging effusion after any withdrawal
Residual effusion and whether tamponade physiology has resolved
avoid: Do not dilate or railroad a catheter over a wire not seen inside the pericardial space.
Do not repeat blind passes at the window that just found the heart.
Do not read failure to improve after drainage as proof of misplacement - clot, a second loculated pocket, or another obstructive shock can do that.
references: Ainsworth CD, Salehian O. Echo-guided pericardiocentesis: let the bubbles show the way. Circulation. 2011;123(4):e210-e211. https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.110.005512

Tsang TS, et al. Consecutive 1127 therapeutic echocardiographically guided pericardiocenteses: clinical profile, practice patterns, and outcomes spanning 21 years. Mayo Clin Proc. 2002;77(5):429-436. https://doi.org/10.4065/77.5.429
European Society of Cardiology. 2025 ESC Guidelines for the management of myocarditis and pericarditis. Eur Heart J. 2025;46(40):3952-4041. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf192
Verify local institutional policy, the pericardiocentesis set stocked in your department, and the surgical escalation pathway.

title: No return of circulation after thoracotomy
trigger: Chest open and still no organized cardiac activity, pulse, or measurable pressure after the incision, the pericardiotomy, or the aortic cross-clamp.
immediateMoves: Work the recoverable technical failures below, in order, before reaching the endpoint.
Exposure: the commonest failure is a small incision. Extend it from the sternal edge to the table, and across the sternum to a clamshell for right-sided injury or wider access.
Confirm the pericardium is open. A tamponaded pericardium is tense and hard to pinch up: grasp, incise longitudinally anterior to the phrenic nerve, evacuate clot.

Find the cardiac wound: posterior surface and great vessels, lifting the heart carefully. Finger pressure first, then a Foley balloon, staples, or sutures. Do not tie a suture around a coronary artery.
Lung hilum bleeding, or air in the coronaries: clamp or twist the hilum. Aspirate air from the left ventricular apex and aortic root.
Two-handed internal cardiac massage throughout, with blood products running.
Internal defibrillation only for a shockable rhythm, at internal-paddle energy, commonly about 10-20 J. Confirm it against the paddle and defibrillator instructions.
Clamp on and nothing changed: question the clamp. It is probably on the esophagus (check by feel against the orogastric tube), or the bleeding is above it.
In a clamshell, expect brisk bleeding from the divided internal mammary arteries when circulation returns. Check the sternal edges first and ligate.
reassess: Organized cardiac activity and a perfusing rhythm
Incision truly runs from the sternum to the table
Pericardium open and decompressed, not only incised over a tense sac
Aortic clamp position under direct vision and by feel against the orogastric tube. Clamp time said out loud every five minutes
Sternal edges for internal mammary bleeding once circulation returns
Blood product delivery, and whether the theater and surgeon are still a real destination
avoid: Do not keep massaging through an inadequate incision.
Do not accept 'pericardium opened' without evacuated clot and a decompressed sac.
Do not leave a clamp on that has not been identified under direct vision and by feel against the orogastric tube.
Do not carry on past the endpoint: no organized cardiac activity after tamponade release, hemorrhage control, and an aortic clamp.
references: Burlew CC, et al. Western Trauma Association critical decisions in trauma: resuscitative thoracotomy. J Trauma Acute Care Surg. 2012;73(6):1359-1363. https://doi.org/10.1097/TA.0b013e318270d2df

Seamon MJ, et al. An evidence-based approach to patient selection for emergency department thoracotomy: a practice management guideline from the Eastern Association for the Surgery of Trauma. J Trauma Acute Care Surg. 2015;79(1):159-173. https://doi.org/10.1097/TA.0000000000000648
Western Trauma Association. Adult Emergency Resuscitative Thoracotomy Algorithm and Procedure Guide. 2024. https://westerntrauma.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/ERT-Algorithm-Procedures.pdf
Verify the institutional trauma algorithm that governs signs of life, CPR windows, and termination, and confirm the tray holds a sternal-division instrument and compatible internal paddles.
